The first call wins: response time in emergency plumbing

When water is on the floor, customers book the first company that answers and gives them a time. What that means for marketing spend and phone coverage.

Emergencies follow different rules

A homeowner planning a bathroom remodel will compare three quotes. A homeowner with a burst pipe will call until someone answers. In emergency plumbing, response time isn’t one factor among many; it is usually the deciding one.

That changes how emergency marketing should be planned, measured and staffed.

It also explains a frustration many owners share: emergency campaigns that look expensive on paper. Often the campaign is fine. The calls arrive, but too many of them arrive when nobody can pick up, and the cost of those unanswered calls lands on the marketing budget. Before judging the channel, look at what happened to the calls it produced.

What we see in emergency call data

  • Callers move fast. If the first call isn’t answered, the next call is usually to a competitor, not a voicemail.
  • Certainty beats price. A clear arrival window on the first call often wins over a cheaper quote later.
  • Night and weekend calls are worth more. They are also the most likely to go unanswered.

“In an emergency, the job goes to the first company that answers and gives a time.”

What it means for your marketing

Only advertise when you can answer

Running emergency ads overnight with no one to pick up is paying to send customers to competitors. Schedule emergency campaigns to match real coverage, or invest in coverage before increasing spend.

Give the call-taker a script that books

The goal of the first call is a booked arrival window. Train the person answering to confirm the address, explain the call-out fee clearly and give a time. Long qualification can come later.

In practice · Plumbing

A two-minute emergency script: name, address, what’s happening, call-out fee, arrival window, and a text confirmation sent while still on the line.

Measure emergency campaigns on answer rate

A campaign that brings plenty of calls but a poor answer rate is not a good campaign, even if the cost per call looks low. Track answered calls and booked jobs for emergency campaigns separately from planned work.

Questions to ask of every emergency campaign
QuestionWhere to find the answer
What share of calls were answered?Call tracking or phone system logs
How many answered calls booked a visit?CRM or dispatch board
When did unanswered calls happen?Missed calls by hour
What did booked jobs earn?Invoices joined to source

Cover the hours that matter

Most plumbing companies can’t staff the phones around the clock, and they don’t need to. Start with the windows that combine high demand and high value: evenings, weekend mornings and the first cold nights of winter. An answering service with access to the on-call schedule can book arrival windows when the office is closed.

Whatever the setup, test it regularly. Call your own emergency number at 10pm on a Saturday and listen to what a customer hears. If it’s a voicemail greeting recorded years ago, that’s the most valuable fix on your list.

Finally, connect the dots back to marketing. When answer rates rise, emergency campaigns can often scale profitably; when they fall, extra budget mostly buys more missed calls. Review the two together every month so spend follows the coverage you can actually provide.

A practical next step

  1. Compare your emergency ad schedule to who actually answers at those hours.
  2. Pause or reduce emergency spend in windows with no reliable cover.
  3. Write and rehearse a first-call script that ends with an arrival time.

Key takeaways

  • Emergency callers rarely wait for a callback.
  • An arrival window booked on the first call beats a lower price.
  • Emergency campaigns should only run when someone can answer.
  • Measure answer rate for emergency campaigns separately.
